owner.occupation: Board-game café owner and hobbyist game designer

world.bio: I taught high-school history for eleven years in Round Rock, then opened a board-game café on Austin's east side with my savings and a small loan. We have about four hundred games on the shelves, a decent espresso machine, and a back room where people test unfinished designs. In my free time I'm designing a trading game about the 19th-century Fuzhou tea route, a project that has taken three years and has been played by nobody outside my Tuesday group.
skills_assets: Board-game café on Austin's east side with a separate back room for playtests
A Tuesday-night playtest group of about fifteen regulars
A complete paper prototype of the tea-trade game: a board, 90 cards, 60 wooden tokens
Eleven years of classroom history teaching: can write clear rules and cheap handouts
A small mailing list of 1,300 players and a Discord with 400 members
Basic Kickstarter know-how from helping two friends fund smaller games

projects.name: Tea Road (working title)
projects.text: A trading game for 2 to 5 players set on the Fuzhou to London tea route, 1860 to 1880. Players buy chests in Fuzhou, pick ships, risk the monsoon and the Cape, and sell in London when the new-season price lands. The mechanics are solid after about forty playtests. The setting is the weak point. Playtesters keep saying the history feels 'Wikipedia-thin', and a US printer quoted $38 per copy for 2,000 units with custom tea-chest pieces, which would put the retail price around $90. Kickstarter is planned for March 2027.

projects.name: Café second-year plan
projects.text: Rent is up again. The back room is my best underused asset; I'm trying to find ways to fill weekday afternoons without a second employee.

projects.name: Half-marathon training
projects.text: Austin Half in February. I've reached eight miles without stopping, mostly in the dark before the café opens.

notes.text: Tuesday playtest. Eight of us. Priya said, again, 'it feels like a spreadsheet with a sailing boat'. I pushed back for about four minutes and then went home and wrote down what she said. She is right. Mechanics fine, flavor thin. The cards that say 'Storm at the Cape, lose one chest' make nobody feel anything.

Got the quote from the printer in Ohio: $38 a copy for 2,000, custom wooden tea-chest tokens, linen box. I did the maths on the back of a menu. After fees and shipping I'd need to sell at $90 to have any margin. Nobody will pay $90 for a game from an unknown designer. Need either a cheaper manufacturer or fewer custom parts.
AC in the café is broken again. Landlord says Thursday. Landlord said Thursday last Thursday. Customers sit with iced coffees and a damp fan. I put out a cheap sign, 'We are suffering with you.'
Coaching niece's chess club. Eleven kids; nine are very good at losing quickly. The tenth beat me in nineteen moves and asked if I wanted to see where I went wrong. I did.

Read a paper on the Fuzhou tea trade because I found it in the footnotes of a book. Prices at Foochow vs Mincing Lane, the clippers racing for the first chests. This is exactly the kind of thing the game should have: real numbers, real ships, real risk. I don't have access to the underlying data, the paper only gives averages.

Monday afternoons the back room is empty. Staff of three, no events. The acoustic panels I put up last year for playtests are still the best thing I've ever bought. Wondering if somebody else could use the room. A language group, a meetup, anyone.
Tuesday group left a note on the corkboard: 'Dan: can we please stop teaching the Opium Wars in the rulebook.' I'm not sure if that was the group or somebody passing through.
Ran six miles. Right knee told me to stop at five. Did the last mile anyway. This is not wisdom.
Started drafting the Kickstarter page. Hated every sentence. Deleted. Opened a bottle of ginger beer and watched a documentary about clipper ships instead.
Found a 1:1 reproduction of a Victorian tea-chest label online for $9. Printed it, stuck it on my fridge. My wife says it's the tackiest thing in the house and she's right.

Customer asked if the café sells the game I'm making. Told her not yet. She said, 'Oh, you're a designer? What's it about?' First time somebody outside the group has asked, and I stumbled on my own pitch.

messages.text:
Priya: Honest feedback: the economy is fun, the history isn't. Where is the human story?
Me: Where would you put one?
Priya: A merchant who loses everything. A captain who bets on a monsoon. Something.

Landlord: AC guy comes Thursday.
Me: You said that last week.
Landlord: Supply chain.
Me: My customers are melting.

Emma: Uncle Dan, can I bring my friend to chess?
Me: Yes, but she has to be okay with losing.
Emma: She's not.
Me: Then she'll learn.

Marcus: I'd go with a smaller print run and a cheaper token set.
Me: Then it stops looking like a tea chest.
Marcus: Customers don't pay for tea chests, they pay for a good game.
Me: Some of them pay for tea chests.

calendar.event: Tuesday playtest, version 0.9 of the market cards
Goal: finish Tea Road prototype v1.0

relations.about: Regular, a software engineer who plays every Tuesday and critiques with a scalpel
Designer friend in Denver who has funded two games
Niece, twelve, runs the school chess club's best players

constraints: The café needs to stay open six days a week, so design time is mornings and Tuesday nights
Not willing to ship a game with invented history if real history is available
Budget for the first print run cannot exceed the Kickstarter's expected funding
sensitive: Personal savings are down to about four months of rent
Worried the game will never be finished and he will have wasted three years
